Bacterial Blight.description: A serious bacterial disease caused by Xanthomonas citri pv. malvacearum affecting leaves, stems, and bolls.
common_symptoms: Water-soaked angular leaf spots delimited by leaf veins
Lesions turning dark brown to black (angular leaf spot stage)
Blackening of leaf veins ('black vein' stage)
Stem lesions causing black arm and seedling blight
general_management: Use certified disease-free and acid-delinted seeds
Treat seeds with approved bactericides/fungicides prior to planting
Maintain adequate field drainage and avoid overhead irrigation
Rotate crops with non-host plants to reduce bacterial carryover
Destroy and plow under infected crop residue after harvest

Curl Virus.description: Cotton Leaf Curl Virus (CLCuV) is a begomovirus transmitted by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) leading to severe stunting and yield reduction.
common_symptoms: Upward or downward leaf curling and leaf thickening
Prominent vein swelling and enations (outgrowths) on underside of veins
Dark green, brittle leaves with shortened internodes
Severe plant stunting and reduced boll production
general_management: Plant certified leaf curl virus-resistant cotton cultivars
Manage vector whitefly populations through integrated pest management (IPM)
Eradicate alternative weed hosts (e.g., Abutilon, Solanum species) near field borders
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which attracts sucking pests
Maintain proper field hygiene and observe regional planting windows

Healthy Leaf.description: Normal, healthy cotton foliage showing standard leaf vigor, uniform pigmentation, and no symptoms of pathogenic infection or pest infestation.
common_symptoms: Uniform green pigmentation across the leaf blade
Smooth, unblemished leaf lamina with well-formed veins
No discoloration, chlorosis, curling, necrosis, or insect feeding signs
general_management: Maintain balanced N-P-K fertilization and adequate micro-nutrients (Boron, Zinc)
Practice optimal irrigation schedule avoiding waterlogging or drought stress
Regularly scout crops for early pest or disease signs
Preserve natural beneficial predators and pollinators

Herbicide Growth Damage.description: Physiological injury caused by drift, volatilization, or soil persistence of non-selective or growth-regulator herbicides (e.g., 2,4-D, dicamba, or glyphosate).
common_symptoms: Severe leaf strapping, feathering, and epinasty (stem twisting)
Chlorotic banding or yellowing along midrib and secondary veins
Malformed, cup-shaped, or fan-shaped foliage with stunted terminal buds
Brittle petioles and delayed flowering
general_management: Use dedicated spray equipment and thoroughly clean sprayers between applications
Apply herbicides under low-drift environmental conditions (optimal nozzle pressure, low wind)
Avoid spraying during high-temperature inversion conditions
Maintain buffer zones between sensitive cotton and adjacent treated fields
Provide supplemental irrigation and mild fertilization to encourage recovery if injury is minor

Leaf Hopper Jassids.description: Damage caused by sap-sucking nymphs and adults of cotton leafhoppers / jassids (Amrasca biguttula biguttula).
common_symptoms: Yellowing or pale chlorosis along outer leaf margins
Upward curling of leaf margins ('hopper burn')
Leaf margins turning reddish-brown and necrotic/brittle
Heavy infestation leading to leaf drop and stunted plant vigor
general_management: Scout underside of leaves regularly for yellow-green wedge-shaped nymphs
Adopt hairy/pubescent cotton varieties that deter jassid feeding
Conserve generalist predators like spiders, ladybird beetles, and lacewings
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor adult jassid populations
Apply recommended organic deterrents (e.g., neem seed kernel extract) at threshold

Leaf Redding.description: A physiological disorder caused by low temperatures, magnesium/nitrogen deficiency, waterlogging, or severe moisture stress, triggering anthocyanin accumulation.
common_symptoms: Red, bronze, or purplish discoloration of leaves starting from margins
Interveinal reddening while major veins initially remain greenish
Premature leaf aging, desiccation, and shedding
Reduced photosynthesis resulting in smaller bolls
general_management: Apply foliar sprays of magnesium sulphate (MgSO4) and urea if deficiency is suspected
Improve soil drainage and avoid prolonged water stagnation around roots
Maintain balanced nutrition with potassium and secondary nutrients
Ensure proper irrigation to prevent abrupt moisture stress during boll development
Choose varieties adapted to local micro-climatic fluctuations

Leaf Variegation.description: Foliar discoloration featuring irregular patches of green, yellow, or white due to genetic mutations, chimeric traits, or localized nutrient imbalances.
common_symptoms: Irregular chlorotic or albino blotches on leaf blades
Patterned or mottled coloring without fungal/bacterial necrosis
Slightly uneven leaf texture without enations or viral vein swelling
Typically localized to specific branches or individual plants
general_management: Distinguish from viral mosaic through laboratory or symptom progression tests
Ensure adequate micronutrient supply (iron, manganese, zinc) to prevent mimic symptoms
Rogue out severely stunted or mutant plants if impacting plot uniformity
Maintain normal agronomic care for healthy non-variegated portions of crop
